reading.rtitle: The Words That Buy You Time
paras: There is a myth that fluent speakers never stop. Record any conversation in your own language and count the pauses: you stop constantly. You say um. You say I mean. You start a sentence, decide against it halfway, and start it again. The difference between that and a beginner stopping is not the number of pauses at all. It is what happens inside them.

A beginner's pause is silent, and silence in a conversation is expensive. After two seconds the other person assumes you have finished and takes the floor. A fluent speaker's pause is full of small words that mean almost nothing on their own: let me think, the thing is, sort of, actually, anyway. Those words are not decoration. They are a hand held up that says: I am still here, do not start.

Sarah teaches business English in Sao Paulo, and she runs the same experiment with every new student. She asks them to describe their weekend, and she counts the seconds before the first silence. Then she gives them eight of these words on a card. Nothing else. No grammar, no new vocabulary. A week later she asks the same question. The average turn goes from about forty seconds to about two minutes, and nobody has learned a single new tense.

In the end, her point is not that these words make you sound fluent, although they do. It is that they make you sound like somebody who is still going to say something, which buys you the four seconds you actually need to find the word. A conversation is not a test with a time limit. It only becomes one when you go quiet, and the other person decides your turn is over.
reading.source: Written for this lesson, from a classroom experiment that any teacher can repeat.

items.situation: You need three seconds to find a word. Say something out loud instead of going quiet.
tips: Let me think. Sorry, what is the word -- the thing you put the coffee in?
Sound is read as: not finished. Silence is read as: your turn is over.

items.situation: You said something badly. Say it again, better, without apologizing.
tips: I mean, it was not bad exactly. It was long.
I mean buys you a second attempt with no cost.

items.situation: Correct something politely, without telling anybody they were wrong.
tips: Actually, it was in March, not in May.
Actually softens a correction into a small piece of information.

items.situation: You went off the subject and you want to get back. Then add something that does not belong.
tips: Anyway, as I was saying, we finished on Friday. By the way, did you get my message?
Anyway comes back. By the way goes sideways.

items.situation: Somebody stops talking too early. Keep them going, and connect their story to yours.
tips: Go on. That reminds me of something that happened to me in January.
Two moves at once: you keep the floor warm and you earn your own turn.

items.situation: Now use four of these words in one answer about your last weekend. Do not go silent once.
tips: Let me think. Sort of a quiet one, actually. The thing is, I had two things on Saturday. Anyway, in the end I stayed home. And you?
Four words, one turn, no silence. That is the whole lesson.

listenings.text: I have lived in three countries, and I have been the worst speaker in the room in all of them. What I learned, very late, is that the sentence you cannot finish is not the problem. The problem is what you do in the two seconds after you cannot finish it. I used to stop, look at the table, and wait for somebody to rescue me. Somebody always did, and then the conversation moved on without me, and I had said nothing. Now I say: sorry, what is the word, and I describe it. The thing you put the coffee in. The room where you wait before the flight. Nine times out of ten they give me the word, and now the word is mine, and the turn is still mine too. Nobody has ever minded. What people mind is the silence, because they do not know whether to speak.

People who study conversation measured the gap between one person finishing and the next person starting, across a lot of very different languages. The average is about two tenths of a second. That is faster than you can decide anything, which means we are not waiting for people to finish. We are predicting the end of their sentence and starting on top of it. It also means that a gap of one full second is enormous, and two seconds is a small emergency that everybody in the room can feel. This is unfair to anybody speaking a second language, because finding a word takes longer than two tenths of a second and it always will. But it explains exactly why the small words work. They fill the gap with sound, and sound is read as: not finished yet. You do not have to be fast. You have to not be silent.
